A year after Claude Code creator Boris Cherny began relying on AI to write all his code, he’s looking to eliminate the time he spends waiting for someone to approve it.

In a post on X on Monday, Cherny described how pull request workflows haven’t kept pace with the speed of AI-assisted development.

Under certain repository configurations, AI-generated code could now reach production without anyone reading it.

Anthropic’s approach could fundamentally change how engineering teams govern software delivery. Under certain repository configurations, AI-generated code could now reach production without anyone reading it.

Shipping without human review

The mechanics behind Claude Ship, currently in beta for Team and Enterprise customers, reveal how Anthropic intends to address a bottleneck that its own coding agents have helped create. Instead of asking engineers to approve every change, Anthropic wants them to decide upfront which changes need a human review.

From writing code to shipping it

The company has been wrestling with the review bottleneck internally for months. Between June and September, the number of merged PRs in the Claude Code codebase more than doubled, while the proportion that required a revert fell by more than 40%, according to an October engineering blog post by Anthropic’s technical staff, Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang.

“We didn’t remove review,” the engineers wrote. Much of the work previously done by human reviewers had shifted to machines, alongside investments in infrastructure that made it easier to reverse problematic changes.

Claude Ship extends that approach beyond Anthropic’s existing multi-agent Code Review tool. PR Steward resolves issues that prevent a pull request from moving forward, while Claude Approvals determines whether the proposed changes satisfy the repository’s approval policy.

Developers can start the process with the /ship command in Claude Code. If administrators enable Claude Ship for an entire repository, PR Steward can push commits to address feedback from human or automated reviewers without waiting for a developer to initiate the process. Existing repository rules and permissions still apply.

Defining what needs approval

Claude Approvals supports natural-language classifiers and Code Review findings in repository-level policies that determine which changes require human approval.

With GitHub’s auto-merge enabled, Claude-approved changes can reach the default branch without human review once all required checks pass.

More sensitive changes still require one or two human approvals, neither of which an agent can satisfy.

At Anthropic, certain low-risk changes can already ship without human approval if they pass automated review and security checks. More sensitive changes still require one or two human approvals, neither of which an agent can satisfy.

When AI review won’t stop

Anthropic encountered a problem with autonomous code review when an internal CLI pull request went through more than 50 rounds of review and remediation overnight before its author intervened. About 59% of the code the reviewer kept flagging had been present since its initial pass.

…an internal CLI pull request went through more than 50 rounds of review and remediation overnight before its author intervened.

“Review has to converge,” the engineering team wrote.

The engineering team subsequently limited its internal review process to three rounds before asking the author to reconsider the implementation. It also narrowed the scope of subsequent reviews to prevent repetitive findings. Anthropic has not confirmed whether the same safeguards apply to every Claude Ship deployment.

What automated review costs

When Anthropic introduced Code Review in March, the company estimated that reviews would typically cost between $15 and $25, depending on the size and complexity of the pull request.

Claude Ship could drive up the cost of automated review if a single PR requires several rounds of inference. Administrators can set review depths and spending limits for individual repositories.

Anthropic has not published standalone performance figures for Claude Ship but internally tracks how long pull requests wait for human intervention, as well as revert and incident rates.
